question: Q11
summary: Published critiques of English-Canadian intellectual history exist and were read in full. The clearest is Clarence Karr, 'What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?', Acadiensis 18:2 (Spring 1989), 158-74. It says it will analyse the field's 'preoccupation with delineating the national mind', its 'propensity to place everything in an atmosphere of crisis', and 'its narrow, elitist, biographical methodology'. Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (Canadian Literature 83, 1979) made a feminist critique: the field was anchored to nationalism and presentism and implied that women were 'virtually non-existent'. Donald Wright (Acadiensis 24:2, 1995) names representativeness as 'the most common charge levelled against intellectual history', after the dismissal of ideas as epiphenomenal. Michael Gauvreau (2010) faulted the field's attention to articulate elites and its national frame; his chapter was checked only through Denis McKim's H-Net review. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) is a real critique of the linguistic turn in social history, but not a checked critique of this field. Quest of the Folk has a published critical forum (Acadiensis 35:1, 2005); Marquis challenges its selectivity and its reach. Owram 1989 is a self-assessment, not a critique.

sources.citation: Clarence Karr, "What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?", Acadiensis 18, no. 2 (Spring 1989): 158-174 (review essay).
sources.argument: Writing as social history expanded, Karr notes that recent commentary calls intellectual history 'in eclipse'. He says social history 'has attracted the brightest of the young scholars' while intellectual history 'remains placid, seemingly oblivious to any methodological deficiencies'. He analyses three attributes: its 'preoccupation with delineating the national mind', its 'propensity to place everything in an atmosphere of crisis', and 'its narrow, elitist, biographical methodology' (p. 160). The group-biography method that followed Berger's Sense of Power focuses on 'an elite group composed primarily of academics, journalists and clergymen' and leaves 'little ... known about the thought of the Canadian population in general' (p. 169). He also asks how representative the chosen individuals were. Targets named include Berger, McKillop, Cook, Shortt, Levitt, Allen and Francis's Underhill. He calls the individual books 'excellent studies within their self-imposed context'.
key_quotes: the focus of Canadian intellectual history has been on an elite group composed primarily of academics, journalists and clergymen (p. 169)

sources.citation: Susan Mann Trofimenkoff, "Nationalism, Feminism & Canadian Intellectual History", Canadian Literature 83 (Winter 1979): 7-20 (special issue on intellectual history).
sources.argument: Trofimenkoff argues that Canadian intellectual history dates from the Quiet Revolution and was anchored to nationalism. Its present-minded interest in national unity left women little room: 'The image they have given us is that the nation is all important ... At the same time they have implied that women are virtually non-existent.' She notes that 'Most intellectual historians have been men' and that women's history grew from social history 'in isolation from intellectual history'. She urges intellectual historians to take up feminist ideas (patriarchy, relations between the sexes) and women's role in forming ideology. Her examples are mostly French-Canadian, but her critique covers Canadian intellectual history in general, including Cook, Berger and Shortt.
sources.note: Karr (1989, n. 6) cites it as a critique on presentism; Karr's footnote gives the issue as '93', but the UBC journal record is no. 83.

sources.citation: Donald Wright, "Discourse, Power and Tradition: Approach and Method in Recent English-Canadian Intellectual History", Acadiensis 24, no. 2 (Spring 1995): 122-134 (review essay).
sources.kind: historiographical review naming the charges against the field (partly a defence)
sources.argument: The essay reviews Valverde, Vipond, Ferguson, Christian and Horton, among others, as three approaches: discourse analysis, the history of political thought and biography. Wright states: 'After the dismissal of ideas as epiphenominal to demographic and economic forces, the most common charge levelled against intellectual history is that of representation' (p. 132). He concedes that the history of political thought 'tends to focus on elites' and cites Karr on group biography. He also cites Owram's reply that representativeness is a problem for all historians. He praises Valverde for avoiding a 'descent into discourse', an echo of Palmer's title. He concludes that 'ideas matter'.

sources.citation: Michael Gauvreau, "Beyond the Search for Intellectuals: On the Paucity of Paradigms in the Writing of Canadian Intellectual History", in Gerald Friesen and Doug Owram, eds., Thinkers and Dreamers: Historical Essays in Honour of Carl Berger (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2010), 53-90. DOI 10.3138/9781442690165-004.
sources.kind: critique of the field from within
sources.argument: According to Denis McKim's H-Canada review (September 2011), the essay 'takes Canada's intellectual historians to task for their abiding interest in articulate elites, and for their commitment to an interpretive approach that is circumscribed by the boundaries of the Canadian nation-state'. These traits, Gauvreau charges, kept the field from engaging with social history and with transnational frameworks. He credits recent work on churches and governments, and wider international framing, for moving beyond them.
sources.date_note: Crossref and OpenAlex give 2010; H-Net's header gives 2009; OpenLibrary gives 2011; the graph's Work node has 2011.

volume_phd_citations_2009_2026.note: Thinkers and Dreamers as a whole

sources.citation: Doug Owram, "Intellectual History in the Land of Limited Identities", Journal of Canadian Studies 24, no. 3 (Fall 1989): 114-128. DOI 10.3138/jcs.24.3.114.
sources.argument: The abstract (Crossref) says intellectual history 'came into its own' while 'limited identities' was influencing the profession. Its roots 'tend to be nationalist in perspective'. Regional differences are 'most apparent in the differing methods and perspectives of francophone and anglophone writers'. Intellectual history 'tends to conform to the historical mythologies of the particular region'. Region matters less here than in many other sub-disciplines. The article appears in a JCS 24:3 special issue on intellectual and cultural history (introduction by Lamonde), alongside McKillop, Fingard, Francis, Cole, Lamonde, Woolf and McGregor.
sources.use: Supports the draft's English-Canadian/francophone split (scope note), not a critique sentence.

sources.citation: A. B. McKillop, "Culture, Intellect, and Context", Journal of Canadian Studies 24, no. 3 (Fall 1989): 7-31. DOI 10.3138/jcs.24.3.7.
sources.argument: Surveying writing on Ontario, McKillop finds a 'pluralistic and significant historiographical field'. Yet 'relatively few mainstream historians ... have written cultural history'. He calls for 'more systematic and theoretical attention to cultural process and transformation'. He argues that organizing the field by provincial or regional boundaries diminishes that capacity.

sources.citation: A. B. McKillop, "Nationalism, Identity and Canadian Intellectual History", Queen's Quarterly 81 (1974): 533-550; reprinted in McKillop, Contours of Canadian Thought (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1987), 1-17 (DOI 10.3138/9781442623309-002).
sources.verification: metadata_checked (Crossref for the 1987 chapter; QQ citation from Bumsted 1977 n.1); text not read

sources.citation: Maria Tippett, "The Writing of English-Canadian Cultural History, 1970-85", Canadian Historical Review 67, no. 4 (December 1986): 548-561. DOI 10.3138/chr-067-04-04.
sources.kind: historiographical assessment of the cultural strand
sources.argument: According to Paul Litt ('The Cult of Nation and the Gnat of Culture', Acadiensis 38:2, 2009, 150), Tippett found that most work on arts and letters was by practitioners or scholars of a particular art form. Historians had produced no synthetic overviews, and she urged them to consolidate the field.

sources.citation: Bryan D. Palmer, Descent into Discourse: The Reification of Language and the Writing of Social History (Philadelphia: Temple University Press, 1990). ISBN 0877226784.
sources.kind: critique of the linguistic/cultural turn in social history (general, not Canada-specific)
sources.verification: book_record_checked; argument from publisher/catalogue summaries and review metadata; text not read
sources.argument: Catalogue and publisher summaries say poststructuralism's reification of discourse obscures structures of oppression and resistance. Palmer insists on the centrality of historical materialism ('language is not life'). Reviews exist in CJH 27:1 (1992, Chad Reimer), JAH 77:4 (1991, Hollinger), AHR 96:5 (1991, Bogue), JSH 25:2 (1991, Bender), J. Econ. Hist. 51 (1991, Amariglio) and Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992, Callinicos); none was read.
sources.use: Not recommended as a critique of this field. Whether the book addresses English-Canadian intellectual or cultural historians is not_verified. Its link to the Canadian field is indirect: Wright (1995) uses the phrase 'descent into discourse' of Valverde.

sources.citation: Acadiensis 35, no. 1 (Autumn 2005) forum on The Quest of the Folk: David Creelman, 'Saying What You Mean: Form and Rhetoric in Ian McKay's The Quest of the Folk' (132-137); Stephen Dutcher, 'Reflections on Modernity and Antimodernism ...' (138-143); Greg Marquis, 'Commentary: The Quest of the Folk' (144-147); Miriam Wright, 'Images of the Fisher Folk in Newfoundland, 1900-1930s' (148-151); Ian McKay, 'The Quest @ 2006' (152-157).
sources.kind: critique of the cultural-history strand's key book
sources.verification: Marquis and McKay full_text_read; others metadata_checked
sources.argument: Marquis questions the book's 'selectivity and applicability for the rest of the region'. He argues that Nova Scotia had 'a countervailing discourse of modernity' from boosters, boards of trade, media and tourism. Citing reviews by Conrad (AHR 1996) and Archie Green (CHR 1996), he also asks how much impact cultural producers such as Creighton and Black actually had, and how far they answered consumers' existing tastes. McKay's reply reports that some readers find the book 'theoretically simplistic' and others 'pretentious and overbearing'. He accepts as 'the most valuable corrective' that antimodernism 'may nonetheless contain more elements of resistance' than his 1994 analysis implied.

sources.citation: Reviews of The Quest of the Folk: Marlene Shore, Labour/Le Travail 37 (1996): 308 (DOI 10.2307/25144053); Margaret Conrad, AHR 101:2 (1996): 596-597 (DOI 10.2307/2170610); Diane Tye, Ethnologies 17 (1995) (DOI 10.7202/1087502ar); Ann McMullen, The Public Historian 17 (1995): 123-125 (DOI 10.2307/3378403); Archie Green, CHR 77:1 (1996): 122-125 (cited by Marquis).
sources.verification: metadata_checked; texts not read (Érudit behind bot check; JSTOR paywall)
sources.argument: Per Marquis (2005), Shore called it 'one of the most important books to be published in Canadian history in years', so her review was not a critique. Conrad and Green raised the question of impact; their wording is not_verified.
sources.note: A folklorist's essay hosted by Athabasca University ('Helen Creighton and the Traditional Songs of Nova Scotia', author not identified in the PDF) calls McKay's claim about Creighton's quest for a mythical folk 'dubious'. Author and venue are not_verified, so do not use it. https://auspace.athabascau.ca/bitstream/handle/2149/1643/Helen_Creighton.pdf

sources.citation: J. M. Bumsted, "Canadian Intellectual History and the 'Buzzing Factuality'", Acadiensis 7, no. 1 (Autumn 1977): 115-121 (review essay; begins mid-page 115).
sources.argument: Bumsted welcomes the field's 'recent blossoming' while noting 'a good deal of confusion'. He proposes Tory, Liberal and Progressive 'Minds' as organizing frameworks, and says all three 'were in their own way elitist' (of the historical subjects, not of the historians). Karr (1989, n. 1) cites Bumsted p. 116 as the source of the 'blossoming' description; the 'most notable for its weaknesses' and 'in eclipse' phrases come from the other works in that footnote (Strong-Boag, CHR 1980; J. D. Wilson, 1984), which were not checked.

not_found: No specific named social historian's published charge of 'elitism' against Canadian intellectual history (for example by Kealey or Palmer in Labour/Le Travail) was located and checked. The charge is documented through Karr (1989), who frames it, and Wright (1995), who reports it as 'the most common charge'.

recommendation.alternative_anchor_2: gauvreau_2010 (only after the chapter itself is read; current support is McKim's H-Net review)
recommendation.cultural_strand_option: quest_forum_2005 (Marquis) for a sentence or a McKay context row, not for the field-level critique
do_not_use: palmer_1990 as a critique of this field (indirect, unchecked)
owram_1989 as a critique (it is a self-assessment)
suggested_wording: Critics charged the field with what Clarence Karr (1989) called a 'narrow, elitist, biographical methodology': group biographies of academics, journalists and clergy, organized around a national mind and moments of intellectual crisis, said little about what most Canadians thought.
Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979) had already argued that a field anchored to nationalism had left women almost invisible.
Optional, if Gauvreau's chapter is read: Michael Gauvreau (2010) later faulted its focus on articulate elites and its national frame.
recommendation.critic_role_option: Karr could be given a critic row (Clarence Karr; Acadiensis 1989). Trofimenkoff is already a CHA president (1984-85) and may already be in the atlas; check before adding.
recommendation.uptake_caveat: All of these critiques are rarely cited in 2009-2026 Canadian History PhDs (0-3 of 1303 each), against 58 for Quest of the Folk and 48 for Berger's Writing of Canadian History. The critique sentence marks a historiographical debate, not a text current doctoral students read.
